subsection: 7. Irish missionaries in Africa and Asia; case study: the Holy Ghost mission to Nigeria, 1945–1966

notes.b: Ireland sent Catholic missionaries to Africa and Asia out of proportion to its population, and this effort was given a national meaning. The phrase Ireland's spiritual empire described the reach of Irish missionaries across Africa and Asia, an empire of faith rather than of territory, and it gave missionary work a national identity.
points: After the Famine the Catholic Church in Ireland was strengthened by the reforms of Archbishop Paul Cullen (Archbishop of Dublin from 1852). Emmet Larkin called this the devotional revolution, a term some historians qualify. It produced a large supply of priests, brothers and nuns.

Irish seminaries (colleges that train priests) and novitiates (houses that train brothers and nuns), such as St Patrick's College, Maynooth, trained far more clergy than the Irish church needed, so the surplus went first to the Irish diaspora (emigrants abroad) and then to the missions.
Irish clergy and religious already served the diaspora in the USA, Britain and Australia, so the habit of sending priests and nuns overseas was in place before the missions to Africa and Asia began.

Irish writers linked the missions to the monks of the early church, such as Columbanus (c. 543-615, an Irish monk who worked on the continent), and to Ireland's reputation as an island of saints and scholars, so modern missionaries could be shown as continuing an old Irish tradition.

Irish nationalism and Catholicism were closely linked, and Ireland had no overseas empire of its own (Britain ruled Nigeria as a colony until 1960). So Ireland could present itself as a leader in spreading the faith without the taint of colonialism.
Irish parishes raised money through collections, missionary magazines and mission exhibitions, which linked congregations at home with the work abroad and kept money and recruits flowing.

Edel Quinn, a Legion of Mary (a Catholic lay organisation) envoy to East Africa from 1936 who died in Nairobi in 1944, became a lay symbol, that is a symbol among people who were not priests or nuns, of Irish missionary dedication.
Mission work gave Irish women a leadership role in nursing, teaching and medicine that was hard to find at home, so it attracted many women.
notes.tip: If asked why Ireland supplied so many missionaries, combine the supply of vocations from seminaries and novitiates, Catholic identity, the absence of any colonial taint, and support from parishes at home.

notes.h: Irish missionary societies in Africa and Asia
notes.b: Several Irish societies and orders ran the missions, each with its own founder, base and field. They are easy to confuse, so learn who founded each one and where it worked.
points: The Maynooth Mission to China was founded in 1916, and it became the Missionary Society of St Columban (the Columbans), with its headquarters at Dalgan Park, Navan, Co. Meath, from 1918.
The Columbans worked in China first, then in Korea, Japan, the Philippines and Latin America, so their field spread across Asia and into Latin America.
The Missionary Society of St Patrick, founded at Kiltegan, Co. Wicklow, in 1932 by Father Patrick Whitney, sent priests to Nigeria and later to Kenya and other African countries.

The Society of African Missions (SMA), founded in France in 1856, had an Irish province (the Irish branch of the society) based in Cork, and its Irish members worked in West Africa, including Nigeria and Ghana.

The Holy Ghost Fathers, called Spiritans, were a congregation (a religious community under a common rule) founded in France with a large Irish province. They took on the missions of Nigeria, Kenya and Sierra Leone, and they are the missionaries of the case study.
The Missionary Sisters of the Holy Rosary, founded by Bishop Joseph Shanahan in 1924 at Killeshandra, Co. Cavan, taught and nursed in Nigeria and other parts of Africa.
Other Irish groups show how wide the movement was, for example the Loreto sisters in India and Irish Jesuits in Zambia and India.
notes.tip: Keep the groups apart: the Maynooth Mission to China (1916) is the Columbans, Kiltegan (Society of St Patrick) dates from 1932, and the Spiritans are the Holy Ghost Fathers. The SMA is a different society, also French-founded with an Irish province.

notes.b: Edward Galvin was a Cork priest who founded the Maynooth Mission to China and became a bishop in Hanyang, central China. His career shows both the energy of the Irish missionary movement and how war and revolution could end a mission.
points: Edward Galvin was born in Co. Cork in 1882 and was ordained (made a priest) for the diocese of Cork in 1909. He went to China as a missionary priest in 1912 and returned to Ireland in 1916.
In 1916, with Father John Blowick, he founded the Maynooth Mission to China, approved by the Irish bishops, which gave the mission the backing of the Irish church.
The first Irish missionaries went to China in 1920, and Galvin led the mission in the Hanyang area of Hubei province in central China.

He became prefect apostolic (head of a mission territory that is not yet a full diocese) in 1924, and vicar apostolic of Hanyang (a bishop who governs a mission territory) in 1927, when he became a bishop.
The mission ran churches, schools, orphanages and clinics, and it trained Chinese catechists (lay teachers of the faith) and priests, so that a Chinese church could grow.
He led the mission through the civil conflicts of the 1920s and 1930s and the Japanese invasion of China from 1937, in which Hanyang was bombed, so war repeatedly shaped the mission's work.
After the Communist takeover of China in 1949 the missionaries faced restrictions, and Galvin was expelled in 1952. He died at Dalgan Park in 1956.

Contemporaries in Ireland saw Galvin and the China mission as heroes of the Catholic church, and their letters and talks raised vocations and money. Chinese Communist authorities criticised the missionaries as agents of foreign influence, and this view shaped their expulsion.
Historians place the Columbans in the wider history of Western missions in China, and they debate how far missionary work helped or hindered local communities.
notes.tip: Give every point a date: born 1882, ordained 1909, mission founded 1916, prefect apostolic 1924, bishop 1927, expelled 1952. Finish with a judgement of his significance.

notes.b: Mary Martin founded the Medical Missionaries of Mary, whose sisters combined nursing and medicine with mission work in Africa. Her order was possible only because a Church rule changed in 1936.
points: Mary Martin was born in Dublin in 1892 and trained as a nurse and midwife (a nurse who delivers babies). She went to Nigeria in the 1930s to work in mission medicine.

Until 1936 the Catholic Church forbade religious sisters to practise obstetrics (childbirth care) and surgery, so a nuns' order could not do this work. A Vatican instruction of 1936 lifted the ban, which is why her order became possible only then.
She founded the Medical Missionaries of Mary, dated to 1937 in Nigeria. The order's mother house (its headquarters) was at Drogheda, Co. Louth.

The order trained doctors, nurses and midwives, and it set up hospitals and clinics in areas where few medical services existed. Nigeria came first, with mission hospitals and nursing schools central to its work, and it later worked in other African countries.
Martin directed the order's expansion and the training of its members, and she became known in religion as Mother Mary of the Incarnation. She died in 1975.
Contemporary Irish Catholic opinion praised the order and its work, so the sisters were presented as models of the mission spirit.
Historians present the Medical Missionaries of Mary as a pioneer of women-led medical missions, and they ask how far medical work served colonial aims.
notes.tip: The 1936 ban and its lifting is a standard point, so link it to Nigeria and Drogheda and give dates: born 1892, instruction 1936, founding 1937, death 1975. Do not confuse her order (1937) with the Holy Rosary Sisters (1924, Shanahan).

notes.h: Case study: the Holy Ghost mission to Nigeria, background
notes.b: The Holy Ghost Fathers, called Spiritans, were a French-founded congregation whose Irish members led much of the mission in south-eastern Nigeria. The mission's early history, and Bishop Shanahan's work in particular, set up the expansion of 1945 to 1966.
points: The Holy Ghost Fathers (Spiritans) began work at Onitsha, on the lower Niger river, in 1885.

The mission area was south-eastern Nigeria, where the Igbo people were the largest group. It lay in the British colony and protectorate of Southern Nigeria and later the Eastern Region, so the missionaries worked under colonial rule.

Joseph Shanahan, an Irish Spiritan born in Co. Tipperary in 1871, arrived in Nigeria in 1902. He made the school the main instrument of conversion, meaning people were brought to the faith through teaching, and built village schools staffed by catechists (lay teachers of the faith).
He became prefect apostolic (head of a mission territory) in 1920 and a bishop, appealed to Irish seminaries for recruits, and founded the Holy Rosary Sisters in 1924.
He left Nigeria in 1931 because of ill health, and he died in 1943. His years from 1902 to 1931 are background only, because the case study runs from 1945 to 1966.
Methodist and Anglican missionaries competed with the Catholics for converts, so rivalry over schools, where converts were won, was a feature of the region.
By 1945 the mission had a network of parishes, schools and a few hospitals in the region, which the postwar expansion built on.
notes.tip: Keep the founders apart: Shanahan (Spiritan, Nigeria, schools, Holy Rosary Sisters) is not Galvin (Columban, China) or Whitney (Kiltegan). Dates to quote: 1885, 1902, 1920, 1924.

notes.b: Between 1945 and 1966 the mission grew into a large network of schools, hospitals and parishes, staffed by Irish missionaries and increasingly by Nigerians. Education was the centre of this growth.
points: After 1945 the mission opened new parishes, schools, hospitals and training colleges across south-eastern Nigeria.

The Archdiocese of Onitsha was created in 1950 when the Catholic hierarchy (the Church's ladder of bishops and archbishops) was established in Nigeria. The Irish Spiritan Charles Heerey became its archbishop, and Joseph Whelan, also an Irish Spiritan, became bishop of Owerri.
The number of Irish priests, brothers and sisters working in the mission rose in the 1950s, with recruits from Irish seminaries and novitiates.

Mission schools became the main route to education in the region, and the Catholic mission ran a large share of primary and secondary schools, so most children who learned to read did so in a mission classroom.
Teacher training colleges prepared local teachers, so the mission could staff more schools, which created a growing educated class in the region.

Hospitals and dispensaries (small clinics that give out medicine) run by the Holy Rosary Sisters and Medical Missionaries of Mary provided medical care in rural areas where government services were few.

The Catholic population of the region grew strongly, and local vocations (calls to the priesthood and religious life) increased. Michael Tansi, an Igbo priest, was ordained in 1937 and beatified (declared blessed by the Church) in 1998.
Nigerians were trained as priests, teachers and nurses, and in 1965 Francis Arinze, aged 32, became auxiliary bishop of Onitsha (a bishop who assists the archbishop).
notes.tip: Name the specific expansion: parishes, schools, hospitals and training colleges, with 1945 and 1950 as dates. Name Nigerians such as Arinze and Tansi to show local leadership, and say only that Irish numbers rose in the 1950s, without a figure.

notes.h: Case study: the mission and the colonial state
notes.b: The mission depended on the colonial government for funding and cooperated with it, though the two sometimes disagreed over schooling and policy. Independence in 1960 then changed the mission's position.
points: The colonial government paid grants towards mission schools under a grant-in-aid system, in return for inspection and standards, so the state could check that the schools it funded reached a set level.
The grants made education cheaper for the mission and for families, but they also tied the schools to government requirements.

Missions and colonial officials sometimes disagreed over curriculum, language and the role of religious teaching in schools, because the mission wanted faith taught while the government wanted set standards.
In the 1950s the regional government of the Eastern Region introduced free primary education, which increased demand for schools and strained mission resources.
Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960, so the mission had to adapt to a new state in which Nigerians held most public offices.
After independence the mission's leadership passed increasingly to Nigerian priests and bishops, a process known as localisation (handing leadership to local people).
Many of the educated Nigerians who served in the new state had passed through mission schools, which gave the mission a lasting role in the country's elite.
notes.tip: Questions on the case study reward the grant-in-aid (grants in return for inspection and standards), independence in 1960 and localisation. Give the free primary education scheme as the 1950s only, with no more exact date.

notes.h: Case study: achievements, criticisms and the Biafran war
notes.b: The mission's achievements in education and health can be set against criticisms of its cultural influence and against the damage of the Biafran war, which is the end point of the case study.
points: Achievements: the mission built schools, hospitals and churches, trained many local teachers and nurses, and helped create a Catholic church with Nigerian leadership.
Criticisms: mission education promoted Christian and Western values, and critics argued that it weakened local culture and languages.

Critics also said the mission was paternalistic (treating local people like children who needed guidance), because Irish missionaries held the leadership long after local people were qualified for it.
Rivalry between Catholic and Protestant missions over schools and converts also divided communities, for example when families were pulled between rival schools.
On 30 May 1967 the Eastern Region declared itself the Republic of Biafra, and a civil war followed until January 1970.

During the war many mission stations, schools and hospitals were damaged, closed or abandoned, and missionaries were displaced. Irish Holy Ghost Father Anthony Byrne was prominent in the relief airlift (food and aid flown in) to Biafra.
The famine in Biafra moved many Irish people, and the Irish relief agency Concern was founded in 1968 in response to it. Concern was a new agency, not part of the Holy Ghost mission.
After the war foreign missionaries left the east, Bishop Whelan of Owerri among them, and the state took over mission schools.
notes.tip: Split your answer into achievements (schools, hospitals, churches, a Nigerian-led church) and criticisms (Western values, paternalism, rivalry). Treat Biafra only as the end point, and do not present Concern as part of the Holy Ghost mission.

notes.b: The missions mattered to Ireland as well as to Africa and Asia, because they shaped how Irish Catholics saw their country. This is the idea behind the phrase Ireland's spiritual empire, and historians judge it critically.
points: Ireland's spiritual empire means Irish missionaries spreading Irish Catholic influence across the world, an empire of faith in place of the political empires of other European states.
Irish Catholics saw the missions as a sign that Ireland was a nation with a mission of its own, not only a country that exported people.
The idea combined Irish nationalism with the universal claims of the Catholic Church, which is why it appealed to both national pride and religious loyalty.
The missions raised money and vocations at home, and they linked Irish parishes to the lives of people overseas.
Later historians have questioned the empire idea, and they see it as a self-image that was closely tied to Irish Catholic identity and to the colonial world.
The decline in Irish vocations after the 1960s and the localisation of the churches in Africa and Asia ended the era of large-scale Irish mission work.
notes.tip: A question on the spiritual empire wants the phrase defined, the reasons Ireland supplied missionaries, and a critical view: it was an Irish self-image, not an empire in the political sense.

notes.b: Judging the missionaries means weighing what they built against what it cost, and separating how contemporaries saw them from how historians see them now.
points: Achievement: the Holy Ghost mission built schools, hospitals and parishes that outlasted colonial rule and produced educated Nigerian leaders and local clergy.
Limit: the mission was tied to the colonial state through grants, it was slow to hand leadership to local clergy, and its work carried cultural costs.
Contemporary view: Irish Catholics praised the missionaries as heroes of the faith, while some African critics questioned their paternalism and cultural impact.
Later view: historians stress both the practical contribution of missions to health and education and the cultural and political costs of their work.

Success was uneven, as these cases show: Galvin's China mission, founded in 1916, ended in expulsion in 1952, while Martin's medical order, founded in 1937, grew in Africa, and the Holy Ghost mission in Nigeria grew strongly from 1945.
For Ireland, the spiritual empire self-image brought vocations and funds at home, and it declined after the 1960s.
notes.tip: State a clear judgement at the start, then balance achievement and limit points, and separate the contemporary Irish view from later historians. Use dated detail such as 1885, 1902, 1945, 1950, 1960 and 1967.
